title: Dynamic hip screw
subtitle: Sliding hip screw for an intertrochanteric fracture

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Hip fracture: management (CG124)

sources.org: Baumgaertner MR et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am 77:1058
sources.title: The value of the tip-apex distance in predicting failure of fixation of peritrochanteric fractures of the hip

sources.org: Association of Anaesthetists (Griffiths R et al). Anaesthesia 76:225
sources.title: Guideline for the management of hip fractures 2020

indications: Trochanteric fractures above and including the lesser trochanter, other than reverse oblique patterns. For these, NICE CG124 prefers an extramedullary implant such as a sliding hip screw over a nail.
Basicervical fractures, and some undisplaced intracapsular fractures, according to local practice.
contraindications: Reverse oblique and subtrochanteric fractures: the screw slides in the wrong direction, so use an intramedullary nail.
Patterns with a deficient lateral femoral wall: many surgeons prefer a nail because the barrel has no buttress.
Pathological fracture from metastasis: needs whole-bone imaging and usually a different construct.
preparation: Surgery on the day of or the day after admission, with correctable problems treated in parallel rather than in sequence.
Anteroposterior pelvis and lateral hip radiographs; template the plate angle against the uninjured side.
Group and save, haemoglobin, renal function; anticoagulant plan documented.
Consent includes fixation failure and cut-out, bleeding, infection, thromboembolism, delirium, limb shortening and mortality.
positioning: Supine on a traction table with a well-padded perineal post.
The uninjured leg in a well-leg holder or scissored down, positioned so the C-arm can reach a true lateral.
Reduce by longitudinal traction and internal rotation, and confirm on both views before preparing the skin.
equipment: Sliding hip screw set with angled barrel plates (commonly 135 degrees) and lag screws.
Angle guide, guidewires, triple reamer, tap and depth gauge.
Image intensifier and a radiolucent traction table.
anatomy: The femoral neck sits at roughly 130 degrees to the shaft and is anteverted, which is why a true lateral view is essential.
Vastus lateralis arises from the lateral intermuscular septum; perforating branches of the profunda femoris pass through near the linea aspera.
The medial femoral circumflex artery supplies most of the femoral head; trochanteric fractures spare it, which is why fixation works here.
The lateral wall of the greater trochanter acts as the buttress the screw slides against.
criticalSafety: Accept no implant until the reduction is acceptable on both views.
Place the lag screw centrally in the head on both views with a small tip-apex distance. A large tip-apex distance predicts cut-out.
Watch the guidewire on screen while reaming: it can advance into the joint or pelvis with the reamer.
structuresAtRisk: Hip joint, from lag screw or guidewire penetration
Pelvic structures, from an over-advanced guidewire
Perforating vessels of the profunda femoris
Pudendal nerve and perineal skin at the traction post
commonErrors: A superior or anterior lag screw position, which predicts cut-out.
Accepting a varus or rotated reduction because it looked adequate on one view.
Losing the guidewire with the reamer and having to re-pass it.
complications: Lag screw cut-out from the femoral head.
Excessive collapse and medialisation of the shaft, particularly with lateral wall failure.
Malunion in varus or with shortening; intra-articular screw penetration.
Surgical site infection, haematoma, venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and delirium.
High peri-operative mortality in frail patients, which is the context for every decision.
postop: Physiotherapy assessment and mobilisation on the day after surgery, with orthogeriatric review.
Regular paracetamol and opioid as needed, no NSAIDs, delirium screening, and a check of haemoglobin.
Bone health assessment and falls prevention before discharge.

steps.emphasis: Traction table with a padded post. Confirm a true lateral is obtainable before preparing the skin; the anteverted neck cannot be judged without it.
Traction plus internal rotation usually reduces the fracture. Check neck-shaft angle on the AP view and that there is no posterior sag on the lateral.
Use the angle guide on the lateral cortex. Aim for a central position in the head on both views and a small tip-apex distance.

step.dhs.approach.title: Lateral approach to the proximal femur
step.dhs.approach.why: The lateral approach reaches the lateral cortex through a single muscle with no internervous plane needed, and it is extensile if the plan changes.
how: Incise along the lateral femur from the vastus ridge distally, sized to the plate.
Divide the fascia lata in line with the skin incision.
Elevate vastus lateralis from the intermuscular septum, or split it, and ligate or coagulate perforating vessels as they appear.
structuresAtRisk: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris
pitfalls: Tearing perforators that retract behind the septum and bleed.
An incision placed too anteriorly, forcing heavy retraction.

step.dhs.ream-lag.title: Measure, ream and insert the lag screw
step.dhs.ream-lag.why: The lag screw is the fixation. Its length and depth decide whether it holds subchondral bone or ploughs out of the head.
how: Measure the guidewire length and set the triple reamer to the length recommended by the system.
Ream under image control, watching that the guidewire does not advance.
Tap in dense bone; insert the lag screw with its tip close to subchondral bone and centred on both views.
pitfalls: Screw stopping short in soft cancellous bone of the neck.

step.dhs.plate.title: Barrel plate application and compression
step.dhs.plate.why: The barrel lets the head-neck fragment slide and impact onto the shaft. The plate must sit flush and aligned or it will lever the fracture into varus.
how: Slide the barrel plate over the lag screw with the keys aligned, and seat it against the lateral cortex.
Clamp the plate to the shaft and insert cortical screws.
Release traction to allow the fracture to impact, and use the compression screw if the system and pattern permit.
pitfalls: Plate not flush with the shaft.
